transcript: This is the Cato Daily Podcast for Thursday, October 22nd, 2015. I'm Caleb Brown. In late 2013, Republican Representative Jim Sen. Brenner unveiled the USA Freedom Act at the Cato Institute's first-ever conference on surveillance. This week, at the second such conference, Democratic U.S. Senator Patrick Leahy discussed the struggles of passing that legislation and what it means for surveillance reform down the road.

I don't even want to try to count the number of meetings off the floor of the House and the Senate, the halls, telephone calls over the weekends. But Republicans and Democrats came together. We passed a bill for the right reason is the right thing to do. And also helps the American people demanded it. It was shocked that the phone records of innocent Americans were being swept up, whether they had any connection to terrorist activity or not. They lost trust in the intelligence community. And they became skeptical of existing legal protection. They demanded meaningful limits on executive authority. They demanded more transparency and more accountability, more checks and balances. And they rallied behind an end to the NSA's dragnet collection of the phone records. These are all common sense things. As Americans, do we really want to give up our basic freedoms for a hint of security. And frankly, that's all it would be, it would be a hint. And there's one other factor. It turned out to be critical. That was the sunset provision. Back in 2001 with the USA Patriot Act was enacted. I joined with thin majority leader Army, Congressman Army. We're not natural allies philosophically, but we were total allies in the sense of protecting our privacy. And we put in a sense of provision of the most controversial surveillance provisions, including Section 215, because we knew if we didn't, It'd be easier never to go back and look at it. Never change it no matter what happens. But if you have a sunset provision, you have to go back to it. We want to force Congress to revisit. That's exactly what happened. So with Section 215 scheduled to expire June 1st of this year, the Senate had not enacted legislation to reauthorize it. The Senate Majority Leader made very clear that he didn't like our bill, even though our coalition in the House and Senate made it very clear we're not going to let a clean reauthorization bill. I think he felt that the time passed, you could say, oh my God, the United States is about to be attacked tomorrow, afternoon at 3.15, if we don't enact this, then some might do it. We fought and, ultimately, because the time had passed, they had to bring up the USA Freedom Act. And we passed with overwhelming support. I don't want to create problems for Senator Lee in Utah, a conservative Republican, but the week before we're out on break and I think we were wearing out the speed dial and our phones back and forth as we were traveling around different parts of the country, lining up votes. I enjoyed working with Mike because he kept his word the whole way through. Now, the USA Freedom Act we enacted in law didn't go as far as the bill two years ago, Congressman Sensenbrenner and I introduced, we both wanted more reforms. But it went much further than people thought we could. We ended the NSA's ball collection of Americans' phone records. We increased transparency of the government's surveillance activities. We're going to declassify a lot more the FISA court opinions, and it's allowed companies like, for example, Yahoo to report more information to the public about government surveillance requests. and to be even more information under the mandatory requirements. I think this kind of sunshine on it, sunshine brought about because of the sunset provisions, the American public would demand even more reforms. And lastly, we enacted major reforms to national security letters. assured they could not be used for ball collection. We strengthened judicial review of gag orders that are used to issue the recipients of it and sells. Told you can't tell anybody why we're seizing all your records. We can't tell. You can't tell anybody why we're looking into your customers. That's not what our Constitution says. And I think history of view of the USA Freedom Act as a crucial step toward recalibrating our surveillance laws. And I think the people worked on Senator Lee, Congressman Sensenbrenner, Chairman Goodlatte, rank and member Connors. Senator Wyden, they supported this. And I want to thank the Cato Institute for inviting me here today. You worked very hard on this. When we had people decided to back away, you helped give them courage. You know, there are some in Congress who want to give our national security agencies a blank check. They think any attempt to protect our privacy somehow makes us less safe. I hear members accept the framework of balancing privacy rights and national security. The privacy rights are preeminent. And we were monitors like our privacy. I'll tell you one quick story. I have very few things over my career that I've actually saved from the press, either favorable or otherwise. But this one I did, I have it framed. And to put this in perspective, I live on a dirt road in Middlesex, Vermont, just outside Montpea. We've had that place for, since I was a teenager, sold a farmhouse. And a neighboring farmer through successive generations have always hated our fields. They keep the hay, they keep our fields clear. It works out well. It's known me since I was in grade school. The time of this happened. Here's the whole article is in the paper. Car pulls up on a Saturday morning with an out of state license plate. Farmer sitting on the porch, the man driving said to Senator Leahy live up this road. He said, are you a relative of his? No, I'm not. Are you a friend of his? Well, not really. Is he expecting you? No, never heard of him. We like our, you know, we like our privacy. We like our privacy. And potentially our basic rights and protecting the country are not part of a zero. some equation. We can do both. But we have to keep in mind, if we don't protect America's privacy and constitutional liberties, what have we given up? Frankly, I think far too much. And I think this great nation has heard if we do. So let's build momentum for more reform, the reform of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, As long overdue, technology is outpaced as live. Originally wrote it back in 1986. Think of what the changes you have in technology and communication since it has overwhelming by price and support. 200 co-sponsors in the house, more than 20 co-sponsors than the Senate. Maybe at the time comes that both bodies start discussing real things. and not slow-geneering, we can get down and actually pass legislation like this. And then, reform the FISA Amendments Act, which, since that's in 2017. There is so much we can't do. I'm not gonna go on to all of the things, but this is important work ahead. But please keep reminding people, just because you want, You keep your rights as an American. Rights that we fought, a revolutionary war, civil war, two world wars to protect. Just because you want to keep those rights doesn't mean you're giving up the security of this nation. I would argue we give up those rights. We've lost the security of our nation.

explicit_propositions.text: The USA Freedom Act was introduced two years ago by Congressman Jim Sensenbrenner and the speaker.
The USA Freedom Act was enacted into law after passing in Congress.
The NSA's bulk collection of Americans' phone records has ended due to the USA Freedom Act.
The repeal of the bulk collection was overdue and represents a significant reform in surveillance laws.
Public outrage followed revelations that the NSA collected phone records without suspicion of wrongdoing.
The American public demanded greater transparency, accountability, and limits on executive power regarding surveillance.
Sunset provisions in the USA Patriot Act required periodic congressional review of surveillance powers.
Section 215 of the USA Patriot Act was set to expire on June 1st, prompting legislative action.
The USA Freedom Act increased transparency by allowing declassification of FISA court opinions and reporting by tech companies.
National Security Letters can no longer be used for bulk data collection, and gag orders now face stronger judicial review.

assumptions.text: Americans value their privacy and constitutional liberties as fundamental rights worth defending.
Government surveillance programs should be subject to regular democratic oversight and renewal.
Fear-based rhetoric about terrorism does not justify mass surveillance of innocent citizens.
Public awareness and moral outrage are essential drivers of meaningful policy reform.
Legislative progress requires bipartisan cooperation despite ideological differences.
Sunset provisions are effective tools for ensuring ongoing scrutiny of emergency powers.
Transparency in surveillance strengthens rather than undermines national security.
Technological advancements necessitate modernization of outdated privacy laws like ECPA.
The judiciary plays a vital role in checking executive overreach in national security matters.
Moral integrity and consistency in governance require aligning policies with foundational American values.
